questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is bleeding after cardiac valve surgery and receives one unit of apheresis platelets. Ninety minutes after it starts, she becomes very short of breath. Temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), blood pressure is 86/54 mm Hg (it was 118/72 mm Hg before), pulse is 122/min, and oxygen saturation is 81% on room air. Jugular veins are flat, and she has crackles in both lungs. A chest x-ray shows new bilateral infiltrates with a normal heart size. Bedside echocardiography shows normal left ventricular function, and BNP is normal. The donor is a woman with four previous pregnancies. Which mechanism best explains this reaction?
choices: Infused volume that exceeds the cardiac reserve of the recipient
Donor anti-leukocyte antibodies binding recipient neutrophils in the lung
Recipient IgE antibodies against soluble donor plasma proteins
Recipient antibodies against IgA in the donor plasma
Cytokines released by donor leukocytes during storage of the platelet unit
questions.explanation: This is **transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)**: **noncardiogenic** pulmonary edema within 6 hours, with **hypotension**, flat neck veins, normal heart function and normal BNP. Plasma-rich products from **multiparous women** often contain **anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies**; they bind recipient neutrophils trapped in the lung, and the activated neutrophils damage the capillaries. **Volume overload (TACO)** is the main alternative, but it causes **hypertension**, distended neck veins and a high BNP.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se de **lesão pulmonar aguda relacionada à transfusão (TRALI)**: edema pulmonar **não cardiogênico** em até 6 horas, com **hipotensão**, jugulares colabadas, função cardíaca normal e BNP normal. Hemocomponentes ricos em plasma de **mulheres multíparas** frequentemente contêm **anticorpos anti-HLA ou antineutrófilos**; eles se ligam a neutrófilos do receptor retidos no pulmão, e os neutrófilos ativados lesam os capilares. A **sobrecarga de volume (TACO)** é a principal alternativa, mas causa **hipertensão**, estase jugular e BNP alto.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has coronary bypass surgery. He asked that his blood come from his family, so he receives two units of red cells donated by his son. Twelve days later, he develops fever, a red rash that starts on his palms and spreads to his trunk, and watery diarrhea. Laboratory studies show high transaminases and bilirubin and falling counts of all three blood cell lines. A bone marrow biopsy shows very few cells. Which processing step of the donated units would most likely have prevented this complication?
choices: Removal of leukocytes by filtration
Washing the red cells with saline
Selection of a donor who is negative for cytomegalovirus
Gamma irradiation of the units
Nucleic acid testing of the donor for viral infections
questions.explanation: This is **transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease**: donor **T cells** survive, attack skin, gut and liver, and destroy the **bone marrow**, which causes pancytopenia. Blood from a **first-degree relative** is a classic risk because the donor may be **homozygous** for an HLA haplotype that the recipient also carries: the recipient does not see the donor T cells as foreign, but the donor T cells still attack the recipient's other haplotype. **Irradiation** stops donor T cells from dividing. **Leukoreduction** is the tempting choice, but it leaves enough T cells behind and does not reliably prevent this disease.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se de **doença do enxerto contra o hospedeiro associada à transfusão**: **linfócitos T** do doador sobrevivem, atacam pele, intestino e fígado e destroem a **medula óssea**, o que causa pancitopenia. Sangue de **parente de primeiro grau** é um risco clássico porque o doador pode ser **homozigoto** para um haplótipo HLA que o receptor também tem: o receptor não reconhece os linfócitos T do doador como estranhos, mas esses linfócitos T ainda atacam o outro haplótipo do receptor. A **irradiação** impede a proliferação dos linfócitos T do doador. A **desleucocitação** é a opção tentadora, mas deixa linfócitos T suficientes e não previne essa doença de forma confiável.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman receives 2 units of red cells after knee replacement surgery. She has had three pregnancies and received a transfusion 9 years ago. Before this transfusion, her antibody screen was negative and both units were crossmatch-compatible. She feels well at first, but on day 8 she returns with fatigue and yellow eyes. Laboratory results: hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL on day 1 and 7.8 g/dL on day 8; total bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL, mostly unconjugated; LDH increased. A direct Coombs test is positive for IgG, and her plasma now contains anti-Jka (Kidd) antibodies. Which best explains why the antibody was not found before the transfusion?
choices: Antibody from an earlier exposure had fallen below detectable levels
Kidd antibodies react only at cold temperatures in laboratory testing tubes
The units were ABO-incompatible because of a labeling error
A completely new primary immune response began after this transfusion
The antibody screen tested the donor plasma instead of her plasma
questions.explanation: This is a **delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction**. Kidd antibodies, made after an earlier pregnancy or transfusion, often **fade below detectable levels** over the years, so the screen is negative; the new transfusion triggers a fast **anamnestic (memory) IgG response**, and hemolysis appears days later with a **positive direct Coombs test**. A brand-new primary response is the tempting choice, but it usually takes weeks and seldom causes this much hemolysis in 8 days. An ABO mismatch would cause intravascular hemolysis within minutes, not a week later.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se de **reação transfusional hemolítica tardia**. Os anticorpos anti-Kidd, produzidos após uma gestação ou transfusão anterior, muitas vezes **caem abaixo do nível detectável** com os anos, por isso a **pesquisa de anticorpos irregulares** é negativa; a nova transfusão desencadeia uma rápida **resposta anamnéstica (de memória) de IgG**, e a hemólise aparece dias depois com **Coombs direto positivo**. Uma resposta primária totalmente nova é a opção tentadora, mas em geral leva semanas e raramente causa tanta hemólise em 8 dias. Uma incompatibilidade ABO causaria hemólise intravascular em minutos, e não uma semana depois.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with colon cancer receives a unit of red cells that has been stored in the refrigerator for 5 weeks. Twenty minutes after it starts, he has shaking chills. Temperature is 40.2°C (104.4°F), blood pressure is 72/40 mm Hg, and pulse is 138/min. He soon bleeds from his IV sites. His direct Coombs test is negative, and his plasma is not pink. A Gram stain of the blood left in the bag shows gram-negative rods. The donor had a mild diarrheal illness a few weeks before donating. Which organism most likely contaminated the unit?
choices: Staphylococcus epidermidis
Listeria monocytogenes
Yersinia enterocolitica
Clostridium perfringens
Salmonella enterica
questions.explanation: Fever, rigors, shock and DIC within minutes, with a **negative direct Coombs test** and no hemoglobinemia, suggest **septic transfusion** rather than ABO hemolysis. *Yersinia enterocolitica* is the classic **red cell** contaminant: it can come from a donor with silent bacteremia after enteritis, **multiplies at refrigerator temperature**, uses iron from the stored cells, and releases **endotoxin**. *Salmonella* is also a gram-negative gut organism, but unlike *Yersinia* it does not grow at refrigerator temperature; *Listeria* grows in the cold but is **gram-positive**, and skin staphylococci mainly contaminate **platelets**, which are stored at room temperature.
questions.explanation_pt: Febre, calafrios, choque e CIVD em minutos, com **Coombs direto negativo** e sem hemoglobinemia, sugerem **sepse por contaminação bacteriana da transfusão** e não hemólise ABO. *Yersinia enterocolitica* é o contaminante clássico de **concentrado de hemácias**: pode vir de um doador com bacteremia silenciosa após enterite, **multiplica-se em temperatura de refrigeração**, usa o ferro das hemácias armazenadas e libera **endotoxina**. *Salmonella* também é um bacilo gram-negativo intestinal, mas, ao contrário da *Yersinia*, não cresce em temperatura de refrigeração; *Listeria* cresce no frio, mas é **gram-positiva**, e os estafilococos da pele contaminam principalmente as **plaquetas**, armazenadas em temperatura ambiente.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man has a femur fracture after a motorcycle crash and receives a unit of red cells. He has had frequent sinus infections since childhood and was treated for giardiasis last year. Four minutes after the transfusion starts, he becomes flushed, wheezes and has stridor. Blood pressure falls from 124/78 to 76/40 mm Hg. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). His urine stays clear, and there is no jaundice. Which laboratory finding is most likely in this patient?
choices: Positive direct Coombs test with IgG on his red cells
Low C1 esterase inhibitor level
Free hemoglobin in plasma with low haptoglobin
Markedly increased BNP
Undetectable serum IgA and antibodies against IgA
questions.explanation: Shock, wheezing and stridor within minutes, **without fever or hemolysis**, describe **anaphylaxis**. Recurrent sinus infections and giardiasis point to **selective IgA deficiency**; such patients can form **anti-IgA antibodies**, which react with the IgA in the small amount of donor plasma left in the unit. **C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency** is tempting because of airway swelling, but it does not cause wheezing and shock with a transfusion. A positive direct Coombs test and free hemoglobin would point to hemolysis, which he does not have.
questions.explanation_pt: Choque, sibilância e estridor em minutos, **sem febre nem hemólise**, descrevem **anafilaxia**. Sinusites de repetição e giardíase apontam para **deficiência seletiva de IgA**; esses pacientes podem formar **anticorpos anti-IgA**, que reagem com a IgA da pequena quantidade de plasma do doador que resta na bolsa. A **deficiência do inibidor de C1 esterase** é tentadora pelo edema de via aérea, mas não causa sibilância e choque desencadeados por transfusão. Coombs direto positivo e hemoglobina livre indicariam hemólise, que ele não tem.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, is RhD-negative. She has just delivered a healthy RhD-positive boy. Her antibody screen (indirect Coombs test) early in pregnancy was negative. Within 72 hours of delivery, she receives an injection of anti-D immune globulin to protect future pregnancies. Which mechanism best explains how this injection works?
choices: It neutralizes anti-D antibodies that she has already made
It coats fetal RhD-positive cells so they are cleared before she responds
It kills maternal B cells that carry receptors for the RhD antigen
It blocks the placental receptor that carries maternal IgG to the next fetus
It provides soluble RhD antigen that makes her T cells tolerant
questions.explanation: At delivery, fetal **RhD-positive red cells** enter the maternal circulation. Anti-D immune globulin coats these cells, which are then **removed by macrophages** (mainly in the spleen) before her B cells can make anti-D; this is **passive immunization** that prevents **active sensitization**. It cannot help a woman who already has anti-D, which is why her **negative antibody screen** matters. Blocking IgG transfer across the placenta is tempting, but the injection does not act on the placenta; it prevents the antibody from forming at all.
questions.explanation_pt: No parto, **hemácias fetais RhD positivas** entram na circulação materna. A imunoglobulina anti-D recobre essas células, que são **removidas por macrófagos** (principalmente no baço) antes que os linfócitos B da mãe produzam anti-D; é uma **imunização passiva** que previne a **sensibilização ativa**. Ela não ajuda uma mulher que já tem anti-D, por isso a **pesquisa de anticorpos irregulares negativa** é importante. Bloquear a passagem de IgG pela placenta é tentador, mas a injeção não age na placenta; ela impede que o anticorpo chegue a se formar.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man has 3 weeks of headache, blurred vision and nosebleeds. Fundoscopy shows dilated, twisted retinal veins with hemorrhages. Laboratory results: hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL; serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal IgM spike of 6.1 g/dL; serum viscosity is 6.2 centipoise (normal 1.4-1.8). Bone x-rays show no lytic lesions. He undergoes therapeutic plasma exchange, and his symptoms improve within a day. Which property of the paraprotein makes this procedure especially effective?
choices: It is filtered and cleared by the kidneys within hours
It circulates mostly bound to the outer surface of red cells
It has a much longer half-life than IgG
Its large size keeps most of it in the blood vessels
Most of it is stored in interstitial fluid and lymph
questions.explanation: **Waldenström macroglobulinemia** makes monoclonal **IgM**, a large pentamer that raises blood **viscosity**. Because of its size, most IgM stays in the **intravascular space**, so **plasma exchange** (an apheresis procedure that removes the patient's plasma and replaces it) removes a large share of the total body IgM and relieves hyperviscosity quickly. IgG is the useful comparison: about half of it sits outside the vessels and moves back into the blood after each session, so exchange removes less of it. The half-life choice is wrong because IgM has a **shorter** half-life than IgG (about 5 vs 21 days), not a longer one.
questions.explanation_pt: A **macroglobulinemia de Waldenström** produz **IgM** monoclonal, um pentâmero grande que aumenta a **viscosidade** do sangue. Pelo tamanho, a maior parte da IgM fica no **espaço intravascular**, então a **plasmaférese terapêutica** (procedimento de aférese que retira o plasma do paciente e o substitui) remove grande parte da IgM total do corpo e alivia a hiperviscosidade rapidamente. A IgG é a comparação útil: cerca de metade dela fica fora dos vasos e volta ao sangue após cada sessão, por isso a plasmaférese remove menos dela. A opção da meia-vida está errada porque a IgM tem meia-vida **mais curta** que a IgG (cerca de 5 contra 21 dias), e não mais longa.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukemia has had three pregnancies and has received many platelet transfusions during chemotherapy. She has no fever, no bleeding and no splenomegaly. She takes no heparin. PT and fibrinogen are normal. Her platelet counts before and 1 hour after two recent transfusions were: first unit, 7,000/mm3 before and 9,000/mm3 after; second unit (next day), 5,000/mm3 before and 8,000/mm3 after. Which mechanism most likely explains the poor response?
choices: Recipient antibodies against HLA class I on donor platelets
Recipient antibodies against the platelet-specific antigen HPA-1a
Pooling of platelets in an enlarged spleen
Consumption of platelets by disseminated intravascular coagulation
Antibodies against complexes of heparin and platelet factor 4
questions.explanation: A very small rise **1 hour** after transfusion (here only 2,000 and 3,000/mm3) shows that donor platelets are destroyed almost at once, which suggests an **immune** cause. Platelets carry **HLA class I** antigens, and pregnancies and repeated transfusions cause **HLA alloimmunization**; leukoreduction lowers this risk, and HLA-matched platelets usually work better. Anti-HPA-1a is tempting, but it is the **main** cause of post-transfusion purpura and fetal-neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia, and it is much rarer than anti-HLA as a cause of refractoriness. Her normal PT and fibrinogen, lack of splenomegaly and lack of heparin argue against the other choices.
questions.explanation_pt: Um aumento muito pequeno **1 hora** após a transfusão (aqui apenas 2.000 e 3.000/mm3) mostra que as plaquetas do doador são destruídas quase de imediato, o que sugere causa **imune**. As plaquetas expressam antígenos **HLA de classe I**, e gestações e transfusões repetidas causam **aloimunização HLA**; a desleucocitação reduz esse risco, e plaquetas HLA compatíveis em geral funcionam melhor. O anti-HPA-1a é tentador, mas é a **principal** causa da púrpura pós-transfusional e a trombocitopenia aloimune fetal e neonatal, e é muito mais raro que o anti-HLA como causa de refratariedade. O TP e o fibrinogênio normais, a ausência de esplenomegalia e a ausência de heparina falam contra as outras opções.
